item.title: The Traveling Salesman Problem with non-convex polygonal neighborhoods: A hybrid Iterated Local Search--Block Coordinate Descent approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.33376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Traveling Salesman Problem with Neighborhoods (TSPN) generalizes the classical TSP by requiring a tour to visit a set of regions in the Euclidean plane rather than fixed point coordinates. It has applications in last-mile delivery, surveillance, and remote sensing in precision agriculture. In this paper, we address the Euclidean TSPN with arbitrary, non-convex polygonal neighborhoods---a highly complex setting due to the joint continuous and combinatorial optimization challenges. To solve the continuous subproblem of determining optimal visit points for a given visiting sequence, we propose a Block Coordinate Descent (BCD) method based on solving fast one-dimensional geometric subproblems. Computational experiments demonstrate that BCD computes optimal visit points for a fixed sequence in almost all instances in which optimality is certified, more than six orders of magnitude faster than a commercial solver solving the equivalent Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Programming (MIQCP) formulation. This efficiency enables an effective hybrid Iterated Local Search metaheuristic (ILS-BCD) that thoroughly explores the combinatorial search space at low computational cost. Extensive computational tests on 235 benchmark instances derived from the Generalized TSP (GTSP), with up to 100 neighborhoods, show that ILS-BCD matched or improved upon the best-known GTSP tours in all cases, obtaining strictly shorter tours in 234 instances. On the 80 instances for which optimality is proven, ILS-BCD attains the optimal tour length in all of them, within a relative difference below 0.001%. On 60 larger instances, with as many as 6,325 neighborhoods, ILS-BCD remains competitive up to about 220.
item.dc:creator: Ernesto G. Birgin, Paula C. R. Ertel

item.title: A block coordinate descent method for nonconvex multiobjective optimization under H\"older continuity
item.description: arXiv:2611.33441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a block coordinate descent method for unconstrained multiobjective optimization problems with possibly nonconvex objectives and H\"older continuous gradients, intended for large-scale instances, in which updating all the variables simultaneously is expensive. In each iteration, only one block is updated along a descent direction common to all objectives, obtained by minimizing the maximum of their regularized quadratic models. We show that, unlike the single-objective case, stationarity on each block does not imply Pareto stationarity, and that no method that updates only the blocks of a partition of the variables and is monotone in all the objectives reaches, in general, an $\epsilon$-Pareto stationary point. Therefore, when none of the blockwise stationarity measures exceeds the tolerance, the algorithm performs a joint step across all coordinates and terminates only at $\epsilon$-Pareto stationary points. We establish a complexity bound of $O(\epsilon^{-(\beta+1)/\beta})$ iterations, where $\beta$ is the smallest H\"older exponent, the same order as that of methods that update all the variables, as well as bounds on the numbers of function and gradient evaluations, which also hold with one regularization parameter per block.
item.dc:creator: Lizet Santa Cruz Calder\'on, John Frank Matos Ascona, Vitaliano de Sousa Amaral, Danilo Rodrigues de Souza

item.title: Using block coordinate descent for solving the close enough traveling salesman problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.33448v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Close Enough Traveling Salesman Problem (CETSP) is a variant of the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem in which the salesperson must visit some point within a disk associated with each customer. Evaluating a visiting sequence requires determining an optimal visit point within each disk. This building block of virtually every CETSP algorithm is typically computed either by solving a second-order cone programming (SOCP) problem with a general-purpose solver, which can be expensive, or by discretizing the disks, which sacrifices optimality. We propose a block coordinate descent (BCD) method that computes these visit points exactly, without discretization, optimizing one visit point at a time. We show that the resulting single-disk subproblem reduces to a one-dimensional minimization, and we characterize its stationary points through the roots of a quartic polynomial. Of the three resulting solution strategies, which agree up to machine precision, Newton's method is the most efficient. Compared with an off-the-shelf SOCP solver, BCD evaluates fixed tours more than an order of magnitude faster. Embedded in an iterated local search (ILS-BCD), it finds the known optimal solutions of 720 small benchmark instances and, on 62 large ones, outperforms all heuristics of their original study in 47 and matches the best of them in 11 others. Within the memetic algorithm MA-CETSP, replacing the general-purpose SOCP solver with BCD and adding an exact local search based on the single-disk solver yields a method that, over the best of 20 runs, is better than the original algorithm in 20 of the 62 large instances and equal in the others, and improves on its best published values in 21. BCD is a fast and exact building block for evaluating visiting sequences that can replace general-purpose SOCP solvers within CETSP algorithms and enables searches that would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.
item.dc:creator: Ernesto G. Birgin, Paula C. R. Ertel, Rogerio S. Matos

item.title: Stochastic Optimization with Network Distribution Dynamics via Local Jacobian Approximation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network systems feature complex interactions among agents, whereby local decisions can influence the state distributions observed by other agents through coupled network dynamics. Such endogenous distribution shifts across large-scale networks pose significant challenges and call for distributed and adaptive decision-making pipelines. To address these challenges and collectively optimize a steady-state performance objective, we propose a distributed network-aware decision-response (D-NAD) gradient algorithm. This algorithm enables each agent to approximate network-response sensitivity using only local information (i.e., the Jacobians of local dynamics and objectives) and neighborhood communication. We establish a non-asymptotic closed-loop convergence guarantee and quantify the impact of the Jacobian approximation errors therein. Numerical experiments on a semi-synthetic networked electric-vehicle price--demand problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Cai, Zhiyu He, Michael Muehlebach, Florian D\"orfler

item.title: Stochastic Optimization for Switch-System Identification under Errors-in-Variables
item.description: arXiv:2611.33545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we address the identification of switched dynamical systems under errors-in-variables, where both input and output measurements are corrupted by noise, and the number of operating modes and subsystem orders are unknown. We propose a unified identification framework that simultaneously estimates the subsystem parameters, latent switching sequence, and model structure. The proposed formulation combines a variance-normalized data-fitting criterion with temporally regularized soft mode assignments and sparsity-inducing penalties for selecting the active modes and relevant input-output lags. To solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop an alternating algorithm that incorporates convex mode-assignment updates and proximal stochastic variance-reduced gradient optimization for parameter estimation. While the existing approaches in the literature require exhaustive searches over candidate structures, the proposed method performs structure selection within a single model. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate recovery of the underlying system structure and favorable computational efficiency compared with a generalized total least squares and dynamic programming approach, particularly as the number of candidate structures increases.
item.dc:creator: Yasin Garehmohammadlou, Mohamad Kazem Shirani Faradonbeh, Mohammad Khosravi, Digvijay Boob

item.title: Controllability of the Cahn Hilliard System at Finitely Many Observation Points
item.description: arXiv:2611.33547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study approximate controllability of the Cahn-Hilliard (CH) system with prescribed targets at finitely many points in the spatial domain. Our aim is to design a L^2 control such that given a finite set of observation points and target values, the solution reaches arbitrarily close to the prescribed targets at these points. First we study the associated linearised system using variational methods and then extend the results to the semi-linear CH system using fixed-point arguments. Further, we investigate approximate controllability in more general setting where we allow the control to be measure valued (in specific, Dirac delta type controls). This formulation is more challenging to obtain requisite regularity due to the simultaneous presence of pointwise observations and pointwise controls. Hence we restrict ourselves to the study of linearised CH system and devise a control which exhibits approximate controllability. We achieve this by approximating measure valued control with L^2 controls and showing appropriate convergence.
item.dc:creator: Sheetal Dharmatti, Greeshma K

item.title: Two-timescale variational Q-learning for ergodic risk-sensitive control of Markov chains
item.description: arXiv:2611.33554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a variational Q-learning algorithm for the ergodic risk-sensitive control of a discrete-time Markov chain with finite state and action spaces and an unknown transition kernel. The proposed algorithm is a two-timescale stochastic approximation algorithm, where the slow iteration solves for the fixed point of the multiplicative Bellman equation cast in a variational form, while the fast iteration solves the associated optimization problem over the probability simplex that stems from the variational representation. We prove that the iterates converge almost surely to the risk-sensitive Q-function and maximizing transition kernel. The proof adapts the ODE method for two-timescale stochastic approximation, where we analyze the global asymptotic stability of the equilibria of the corresponding fast and slow ODEs as well as bound the trajectory of the fast ODE away from zero. The main challenge lies in proving that, almost surely, the slow iterates are norm-bounded and the fast iterates are bounded below away from zero on the support of the transition kernel. We address this by using a fluid scaling approach for the slow iteration combined with tailored estimates for the fast iteration to control a certain fluid-scaled relative entropy error that arises in the ODE approximation. Numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithm and compare it with the existing risk-sensitive Q-learning algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Nicola G. Sassone, Guodong Pang

item.title: Solving the capacitated vehicle routing problem with polygonal neighborhoods using a metaheuristic enhanced with block coordinate descent
item.description: arXiv:2611.33583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) in which customers are represented by planar regions, called customer neighborhoods, rather than fixed points. Visiting a customer consists of selecting a point within its neighborhood. Therefore, besides determining the sequence of customers visited by each vehicle, one must also determine the corresponding visit points. To better reflect practical applications, customer neighborhoods are allowed to be simple polygons, either convex or non-convex, and distances are measured using the Euclidean norm. Applications include aerial reconnaissance, wireless sensor data collection and inspection, and two-stage delivery systems. We propose a general variable neighborhood search framework in which each neighbor is represented by a collection of routes. Constructing a route involves two stages, defining a customer sequence and then determining the associated visit points. The latter task is solved by a block coordinate descent (BCD) procedure, the central methodological contribution of this work, which computes high-quality visit points at a cost low enough to be used repeatedly inside the search. In extensive experiments on newly generated and adapted benchmark instances, within the time limits considered, the proposed framework matches all solutions proven optimal by CPLEX and matches or improves the best solutions found by CPLEX in the remaining instances. For the instances adapted from the CVRP literature, it also improves, in every instance, a CVRP-based upper bound given by the solution of the original CVRP instance reported in the literature, which is feasible for the problem with neighborhoods.
item.dc:creator: Ernesto G. Birgin, Rog\'erio S. Matos

item.title: A Stackelberg strategy for the semi-linear heat equation with boundary controls
item.description: arXiv:2611.33683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work continues the results presented in \cite{calsavara2022new} where a hierarchical control problem is solved. Our first goal is the case of both controls acting on the boundary. The follower control solves a null controllability problem, and the leader minimizes a $L^2$ cost functional. Additionally, we solve the case where one control acts on the boundary and the other on an open subset of the domain. More precisely, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a leader-follower couple and give some techniques to solve the problem.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Villa, J.A. A Stackelberg strategy for the semi-linear heat equation with boundary controls. Bol. Soc. Mat. Mex. 32, 22 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Jose Antoinio Villa

item.title: Universal Stabilization with Six Records
item.description: arXiv:2611.33762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This letter shows that a single feedback controller needs only six retained observation records to handle the largest universally stabilizable uncertainty range for the scalar discrete-time benchmark model of Xie and Guo, when uncertainty is measured by the radius of a generalized Lipschitz ball. Existing constructions can require arbitrarily many records along bounded trajectories. Our controller retains at most six genuine state-response pairs and five auxiliary real scalars. Each update requires a uniformly bounded number of elementary operations. No knowledge of the plant, its generalized Lipschitz constants, or the disturbance bound is required.
item.dc:creator: Senhan Yao

item.title: Variance Reduction Note 6: The Convergence of SAGA
item.description: arXiv:2611.33782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: SAGA corrects a sampled component gradient with a table of previously computed gradients. Updating one entry at a time gives an unbiased gradient estimate at the cost of one new component gradient per iteration. This sixth note on variance reduction proves a linear convergence guarantee for a smooth finite sum with convex components and a strongly convex average. A two-component quadratic shows how the spread of the stored evaluation points determines the variance, even at the minimizer. We track the iterate and the table jointly to obtain a last-iterate bound, then relate its dependence on the sample size to the rate at which individual entries are replaced. For generalized linear losses the same gradient table can be represented by one scalar per observation and a running mean.
item.dc:creator: Kamran Fareed, Alina Lodhi

item.title: BGPNP: A Non-Euclidean Gradient Projection Newton Pursuit Method for Sparsity-Constrained Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.33802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A non-Euclidean gradient projection Newton pursuit method is proposed for solving sparsity constrained optimization problem via the Bregman distance. The method is also denoted as BGPNP. The method firstly constructs a gradient projection step based on the Bregman distance to ensure that the iterates satisfy the sparsity constraint. Then, when the support set becomes stable or the gradient norm is sufficiently small, a Newton pursuit step is introduced to improve local convergence efficiency. The BGPNP is proved to possess a sufficient descent property and the non-increasing monotonicity of the objective function values. The full convergence and linear convergence rate of the BGPNP are established under appropriate conditions, which do not involve the symmetry coefficient of Bregman distance and the $\theta$-uniform condition. Moreover, the locally quadratical convergence rate of the BGPNP is also obtained. This method provides an effective algorithmic framework for sparse optimization in non-Euclidean setting. Numerical experiments on sparsity-constrained compressed sensing problems validate the competitive performance of BGPNP compared with existing leading solvers.
item.dc:creator: Jiawei Chen, Huilin Han, Yibing Lv, Jen-Chih Yao

item.title: Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao Reconstruction of Discrete space Population Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.33923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing the continuous time dynamics of cell state evolution from sparse snapshot observations can be formulated as an unbalanced optimal transport problem. To study such dynamics at a coarse grained cell type level, unbalanced optimal transport must be extended to discrete state spaces. Inspired by discrete flow matching, we extended the dynamic Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) problem to discrete spaces, and derived a closed form for its solution. For particularly large state spaces or more general models, we proposed an unbalanced discrete flow matching as a numerical approximation method, which provides a Markovian reconstruction of the optimal WFR flow. Our discrete WFR framework also stays stable across different coarse grain resolution. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed approach, and applications to real biological data supported the plausibility of the reconstructed dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Junda Ying, Xinyu Wang, Peijie Zhou, Lei Zhang

item.title: Near Optimal Pure Stepsize Adaptation Acceleration for Gradient Descent on Nonconvex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.33931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing accelerated first-order methods for nonconvex optimization typically rely on momentum or extrapolation, requiring auxiliary vectors beyond the current iterate and gradient. On the other hand, memory-free stepsize scheduling alone can accelerate certain convex problems, while no guarantee exists for nonconvex problems. This paper closes this gap by proposing Nonconvex Adaptively Clipped Chebyshev (NACC) gradient descent method, which achieves near optimal acceleration while keeping the vanilla gradient descent update. NACC combines an adaptive selection of reversed fractal Chebyshev stepsizes with an epoch-wise clipping mechanism to control the aggressiveness of stepsizes. For nonconvex problems with Lipschitz continuous gradients and Hessians, we establish a near-optimal $\widetilde O(\epsilon^{-7/4})$ complexity. If the problem is convex in addition, then, without modification, NACC automatically achieves an $\widetilde O(\epsilon^{-3/4})$ accelerated complexity. Importantly, NACC guarantees the standard quadratic sufficient descent at every iteration, even when the stepsizes are substantially larger than the conventional choice. These monotonicity properties further facilitate practical implementations that adaptively adjust the estimated gradient and Hessian Lipschitz constants, demonstrating significant advantages in numerical tests against the existing nonconvex acceleration benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Yin Liu, Ziyang Zeng, Junyu Zhang

item.title: Policy and Value Iteration for Entropy-Regularized Stochastic Control
item.description: arXiv:2611.34002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite-horizon entropy-regularized stochastic control with action-independent diffusion. To solve the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation, we alternate between value and policy updates. Each iteration approximately solves a linear backward equation for the current policy, then approximates the Gibbs distribution defined by the resulting value gradient. We prove a uniform bound on the final policy's excess regularized cost. The bound assigns explicit, summable weights to the evaluation residuals and the Kullback-Leibler divergences from the updated policies to their Gibbs targets. Under the stated assumptions and with exact terminal data, vanishing errors in both steps imply uniform convergence to the optimal value. Two finite-horizon execution problems test value accuracy against a known solution and closed-loop performance when no exact solution is available. We also evaluate the iteration on a discounted infinite-horizon routing problem with twelve modes and an unregularized HJB benchmark in up to 10,000 dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Yuling Jiao, Peiying Wu, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Ruizhe Zhang, Tao Zhou

item.title: A Robust Optimization Framework for Energy System Capacity Expansion under Line Outage Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2611.34113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Capacity expansion models are widely used in climate and energy policy analysis to find optimal investments in generation, storage, and transmission. As the share of renewable generation grows, these models rely more on transmission lines to balance supply and demand across regions. Transmission lines, however, can fail due to aging, extreme weather, or accidents. Models that represent outages as time-dependent events come mainly from electrical engineering and are applied to small-scale systems, as they quickly become computationally intractable for inter-regional capacity expansion. We develop a capacity expansion model in which the risk of line failures shapes the investments in all parts of the system. We formulate it as a two-stage, scenario-based robust optimization problem that samples time-varying outage scenarios from a Markov model and hedges the investments against the most severe ones. To solve the model, we propose a memory-augmented Benders decomposition algorithm combined with Monte Carlo simulation that can handle thousands of scenarios. The selected plan is then evaluated with an out-of-sample simulation to bound the Value-at-Risk (VaR) of its system cost. In a 25-node case study of Germany and its neighboring countries, the gap between the lower bound and the simulated VaR bound is below 1%. We compare the robust plans with a deterministic plan, which assumes all lines are always available, and with a reserve-margin heuristic, which requires local firm capacity to be above peak demand. Like the heuristic, the robust plans nearly eliminate loss of load in 1000 simulated outage scenarios. Their mean system cost is within 0.2% of the deterministic plan and about 4.5% below the heuristic. Instead of adding more generation capacity, the robust approach mainly changes the type and location of capacity, for example, by spreading storage across the network.
item.dc:creator: Kamran Forghani, Lina Reichenberg, Fredrik Hedenus, Iegor Riepin

item.title: Scaled Coordinate Descent for Convex Quadratic Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.34123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a modification of coordinate descent for unconstrained symmetric positive definite quadratic programs that combines a coordinate correction with an exact scaling of the current iterate. For a selected coordinate, the method minimizes the objective function over the two-dimensional subspace spanned by the current iterate and the corresponding standard basis vector. Closed-form expressions are obtained for the two update parameters and for the resulting objective decrease. The scaling produces a state-dependent effective curvature that is no larger than the diagonal curvature used by standard coordinate descent, so the exact scaled update makes at least as much progress for the same selected coordinate. We discuss initialization, numerical stability, randomized coordinate selection, experimental comparisons with ordinary two-coordinate descent, and a block coordinate extension. In the spirit of previous theoretical results, we give a probabilistic linear convergence result. Finally, we provide experimental results to show the effectiveness of the proposed method on synthetic data.
item.dc:creator: Cristian Rusu

item.title: A Counterexample to Single-Control Null Controllability of Stochastic Heat Equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.34337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We disprove the conjecture that a single localized drift control suffices for null controllability of stochastic parabolic equations with bounded adapted coefficients. On a bounded interval with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, we construct a deterministic, nonnegative smooth noise coefficient supported at positive distance from the control interval. One fixed nonzero smooth initial state cannot be driven to zero almost surely at any positive time by any progressively measurable control with finite expected $L^2$ energy. The proof uses products of Brownian increments in the adjoint terminal data to keep the initial pairing bounded away from zero while the observation norm tends to zero. On the flat torus, the construction yields counterexamples in every Gevrey class of order $s>1$ whenever the complement of the control set contains an open ball. Thus Gevrey regularity above order one cannot replace analyticity as a general sufficient condition for null controllability.
item.dc:creator: Feizheng Huang, Zhaobo Liu

item.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2611.34419v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.
item.dc:creator: David Krame Kadurha, Alessandro Zocca, Sandjai Bhulai

item.title: The Monge Optimal Transport Barycenter Problem with Adaptive Features
item.description: arXiv:2611.34494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The data-driven Monge optimal transport barycenter problem seeks a map $y=T(x,z)$ that minimally perturbs an outcome $x$ while removing its statistical dependence on covariates $z$. Numerical implementations approximate the independence constraint through finite-dimensional test-function spaces, making the effectiveness of dependence removal sensitive to the choice of features. This article develops a procedure whereby the features themselves are optimized throughout the procedure. In particular, we adopt a feature space for $f$ consisting of Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) with adaptive individual centers and bandwidths. Synthetic experiments show that while fixed nonlinear RBF features can capture dependence structures that are poorly represented by linear features, adapting the RBF centers and bandwidths can further improve dependence removal within a limited feature space and achieve residual dependence comparable to that obtained with a larger fixed basis. We further extend the formulation to multidimensional covariates and evaluate its applicability to real-world problems, including removing age-related dependence in biomedical measurements and dependence on temperature and humidity in bike-sharing demand.
item.dc:creator: Yige Zhou, Esteban G. Tabak

item.title: Efficient Data Fusion in Distributionally Robust Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.34495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decisions under uncertainty increasingly rest on fragmented evidence, such as samples from related but different populations, privacy-protected summary statistics, or complementary statistical descriptions of the same data. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) can fuse such evidence by constructing one ambiguity set per source and hedging against all distributions in the intersection of these sets. This fusion approach is less conservative than aggregating the sources into a single ambiguity set, but it is computationally demanding. Exact reformulations grow exponentially with the number of sources, and even deciding whether the intersection is nonempty is NP-hard. We show that fusion DRO admits an exact reformulation in which the ambiguity sets are coupled only through functional Lagrange multipliers. Restricting these multipliers to affine decision rules yields upper bounds that decompose across the ambiguity sets, are exact for quadratic losses over Wasserstein balls around Gaussian references, and provably dominate aggregation-based relaxations such as Minkowski sums and balls around mixtures. The approximations admit finite conic reformulations in important special cases and subgradient methods for weakly convex losses, which makes fusion DRO applicable to neural network training. In portfolio, newsvendor, and binary classification experiments, the affine approximation stays close to the exact value wherever the latter is computable, scales far better than exact methods, and outperforms aggregation-based benchmarks out-of-sample.
item.dc:creator: Buse \c{S}en, Aras Selvi, Jean Pauphilet, Daniel Kuhn

item.title: Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM Inference: Theory and Implementation
item.description: arXiv:2611.34584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-turn AI agents execute iterative loops of large language model (LLM) inference and external tool calls, transforming cluster serving into a dynamic resource-allocation problem where routing and key-value (KV) cache retention jointly govern prefix reuse across inter-turn delays. We formulate a fluid approximation of this system and show that optimal admission, routing, and eviction are governed by endpoint-specific shadow prices for computation and memory together with session continuation values. Building on this structure, we propose an asymptotically optimal buffer-reserve policy that absorbs stochastic fluctuations using a vanishing share of capacity. To handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed load reports, and engine-local memory management in production clusters, we translate these principles into a practical controller named PARK, which pairs online projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead with a local KV retention index ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch. In real GPU cluster experiments serving a 197-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on multi-turn software-engineering agent benchmarks (SWE and Terminal-Bench), PARK outperforms all five load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting traffic regimes. On 16 H200 GPUs, PARK raises output throughput by $24.2\%$ over the strongest baseline ($336.9\%$ over round robin) on turn-intensive SWE trajectories and by $40.0\%$ over the strongest baseline ($63.3\%$ over round robin) on generation-intensive Terminal-Bench trajectories. Controlled single-replica ablations show that our retention index alone cuts prior-prefix token loss from $13.26\%$ to $2.17\%$ and increases throughput by $36.7\%$ over least-recently-used (LRU) eviction, while 128-GPU scale-up experiments sustain 50,789 to 67,363 output tokens/s across 16~replicas with prefix cache hit rates of $91.3\%$ to $97.4\%$.
item.dc:creator: Sentao Miao, Tianjiao Nie, Yuan Zhou, Song Yuan, Yuanwei Lu, Yibo Zhu

item.title: Sequential Portfolio Optimizer (SPO-CPU and SPO-GPU): C++ Interior-Point Solvers and Differentiable Layers for Quadratic Cone Programs
item.description: arXiv:2611.34590v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quadratic cone programs (QCPs) are a practical canonical form for convex optimization, including parametric portfolio problems that must be re-solved to high accuracy as market data change. We present Sequential Portfolio Optimizer (SPO), with SPO-CPU and SPO-GPU the C++ and CUDA realizations of the Clarabel homogeneous-embedding interior-point method. Clarabel is a registered trademark; SPO is our name for these implementations. Each exposes a forward optimizer and an in-solver differentiable layer. The Mehrotra algorithm is unchanged. The contribution is an implementation stack: a reduced two-block vector-Jacobian product with gradients in the original coordinates; a documented variant of the Chen--Goulart--Jones smoothing warm start, applied in equilibrated coordinates; and a GIL-free GPU batch architecture whose isolated throughput is at parity with a warm solver loop up to $B{=}16$. On an RTX A6000, subsequent solves of a $5000$-asset factor-model QP average $24$ ms on SPO-GPU, compared with $98$ ms on Clarabel.rs and $122$ ms on single-thread Gurobi; at $10{,}000$ assets the corresponding GPU time is $59$ ms against $439$ ms for one-thread Mosek. Clarabel.rs, SPO-CPU, and SPO-GPU agree pairwise to $2.2{\times}10^{-7}$ in relative objective on this family. Against a CVXPYLayers baseline driven by Clarabel, the GPU layer reproduces the solution and the return-gradient on a $5000$-asset factor QP/SOCP, while a subsequent forward-plus-backward step is $101$--$137\times$ faster at $5000$ assets (and $17$--$30\times$ at $1000$ assets). The smoothing warm start reduces QP rebalance iterations but can increase them on a large GPU second-order cone. Wall-clock rankings apply to the factor-model family only; an $18$-problem Maros--M\'esz\'aros subset is reported as a cross-check. We do not claim a speedup over CuClarabel, and the batch architecture is not a measured throughput improvement.
item.dc:creator: Fan Zhao, Yan Zaretskiy, Yuwen Chen, Jerry Shi

item.title: On the Convergence of Discrete-Time Primal-Dual Algorithm for Distributed GNE Seeking
item.description: arXiv:2611.34757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the convergence of a discrete-time distributed primal-dual algorithm for generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) seeking in a class of noncooperative games with nonlinear coupling constraints. We establish semi-global convergence of the algorithm under a fixed stepsize, in the sense that convergence can be guaranteed from any prescribed compact set of initial conditions by choosing a sufficiently small stepsize. Under a diminishing stepsize sequence, we further establish global convergence when the constraints are globally Lipschitz continuous. For the special case of affine constraints, global convergence is also guaranteed under a sufficiently small fixed stepsize. Finally, we extend these convergence results to a fully distributed GNE seeking algorithm in a partial-decision information setting, where each agent only has access to the actions of its neighbors. These results complement existing convergence results for continuous-time primal-dual dynamics, and provide new convergence guarantees for the discrete-time counterpart in distributed GNE seeking.
item.dc:creator: Weijian Li, Lacra Pavel, Panos J. Antsaklis, Hai Lin

item.title: APEX: Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.33450v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ensemble-based methods provide a practical framework for history matching, prediction, and optimization of subsurface models. In methodological studies, however, performance is rarely assessed from a single run. Comparisons typically span cases, configurations, and random seeds, while each evaluation may require an expensive external simulator. Keeping such studies computationally bounded, auditable, and reproducible therefore requires more than implementing a numerical method: experiments must be validated before execution, computational costs estimated, repeated runs organized consistently, and configurations and outputs made traceable. To address these needs, we developed APEX (Agentic Platform for Ensemble eXploration), an open-source Python platform that provides a common framework for configuring, validating, executing, recording, and comparing ensemble-based experiments. APEX is organized around three concepts: an experiment defines what is executed, a run records a single execution, and a study coordinates and compares multiple experiments or runs. Experiments are specified through validated configurations, which can also be generated by a planner agent. Before execution, APEX estimates the maximum number of forward simulations required. If the estimate exceeds a user-defined threshold, submission is held for approval. Each run records provenance information, while studies repeat problems across variants and paired replicates and compare results using paired statistical analyses. Scientific and computational components, including methods, simulators, metrics, and optimizers, are implemented as plugins. A command line interface, Python client, REST service with a web interface, and tools for language model agents access these capabilities through a common service layer.
item.dc:creator: Xiaodong Luo

item.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.33644v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
item.dc:creator: Takuma Adams, Andrew C. Cullen, Tansu Alpcan

item.title: On Grokking and the Dynamics of Generalization
item.description: arXiv:2611.33825v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We extend the signal-channel theory of grokking introduced by Litman and Guo by relating training dissipation and evaluation transfer to population risk. For preconditioned gradient flows with time-dependent kernels, we distinguish two sources of limited evaluation visibility, namely small cumulative dissipation and weak transfer. We obtain quantitative bounds for task visibility and establish their stability under signal filtering and changes of evaluation distribution. We describe how task directions enter the effective signal channel through spectral activation or transport. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the transferred signal to decrease squared population risk and derive classification error bounds under margin assumptions. These results yield sufficient conditions for the same training trajectory to generalize under one evaluation distribution while failing under another. We show that differences in spectral learning rates can produce arbitrarily long delays between low training loss and low population risk. By relating classification accuracy to the distribution of margin crossing times, we construct a family of gradient flows in which the generalization delay tends to infinity, while both the duration of the transition from zero to full accuracy and the corresponding variation of population risk tend to zero. These phenomena occur without feature evolution during training. Finally, we prove that the occurrence and timing of generalization cannot generally be inferred from training dynamics alone, but depend on the geometry of evaluation transfer and its relation to the target.
item.dc:creator: Malik Amir

item.title: Concavity of cardinality-constrained interval stabbing and interval cover problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.34089v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the cardinality-constrained interval stabbing problem, in which the goal is to maximize the total weight of intervals hit by at least one of at most $k$ selected points. Although this problem does not admit a simple greedy solution, we show that its optimal value is a concave function of $k$. We establish this result using a linear programming formulation whose relaxation always admits an optimal solution with integer values. This allows us to prove concavity for the original problem. We further extend the result to the related interval cover problem. These concavity properties provide a basis for applying Lagrangian optimization using algorithms for the corresponding unconstrained problems.
item.dc:creator: Janez Brank, Toma\v{z} Ho\v{c}evar

item.title: Time-consistency of cash-subadditive risk measures: The infimal cocycle property
item.description: arXiv:2611.34192v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We characterize the time-consistency of convex, cash-subadditive dynamic risk measures in terms of their minimal penalty. The dual variables are conditional sub-probability densities, which factorize across an intermediate date in many ways, according to how the discount is allocated to the two periods. We introduce an infimal cocycle property, in which the penalty is the infimum over all such factorizations, and show that it is equivalent to time-consistency, with the infimum attained. This holds on $L^\infty$ under continuity from below, and on $L^p$, $p<\infty$, without continuity assumptions. In the cash-additive case it reduces to the classical cocycle property. For risk measures induced by BSDEs, it represents the dynamic programming principle of a stochastic control problem whose value is the penalty.
item.dc:creator: Matteo Ferrari, Roger J. A. Laeven, Emanuela Rosazza Gianin, Marco Zullino

item.title: Prophet Inequalities for Mixtures of I.I.D. Random Variables
item.description: arXiv:2611.34264v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A latent index $J\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ is drawn from a prior $\pi$. Conditional on $J=j$, a gambler observes random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ drawn independently from a non-negative component distribution $F_j$. The gambler knows $n$, the prior $\pi$, and the component distributions $F_1,\ldots,F_k$, but not $J$, observes the values sequentially, and selects at most one value at the time it is revealed. We show that the largest $\alpha$ such that the gambler can guarantee to select a value of $\alpha\cdot\mathbb{E}[\max_iX_i]$ in expectation, for all distributions where this expectation is finite, is \[ \alpha=\frac1e+\frac{1}{k^{2/3+o(1)}}. \] The lower bound is achieved by the better of two variants of the standard secretary rule. The upper bound uses a finely tuned instance of the common-scale model, which scales a sequence of independent random variables by a single latent variable.
item.dc:creator: Felix Fischer, Kevin Schewior

item.title: Mean field game value multifunction: dynamic programming principle
item.description: arXiv:2611.34268v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study mean field games (MFGs) on the torus with non-degenerate diffusion, in a regime (no monotonicity) where multiple solutions exist for the same data. In this setting the value of a representative player is not a function of the initial time and distribution, and the classical master equation loses its meaning. We describe the dependence of the value on the initial data by a multivalued mapping, the value multifunction, assigning to each initial time and distribution the set of value functions of all solutions of the MFG starting from that data. Our main result gives a sufficient condition for a closed multifunction to be a value multifunction, namely, it must satisfy a dynamic programming principle formulated on proper time subintervals, expressed as invariance of its graph under the forward operators generated by equilibria of the game. This replaces the global requirement that each value be produced by a solution of the forward-backward system on the whole time interval by a local, time-consistent condition together with closedness, which carries the terminal condition. The result is the second-order analogue of the viability approach previously developed for first-order mean field games. We reformulate solutions of the mean field game in terms of relaxed equilibria, show that the closure of a value multifunction is again a value multifunction, and prove that the forward operators compose as a semigroup. We also present an explicit example in which a single terminal cost produces at least two solutions for every initial time in an interval, while solutions are unique for initial times sufficiently close to the horizon.
item.dc:creator: Y. Averboukh, S. Mayorga

item.title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.34452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a core task in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Physics-informed neural networks and the deep Galerkin method effectively leverage machine learning models to approximate solutions of known PDEs by minimizing residuals corresponding to the PDE operator alongside external constraints. Although second-order optimizers are becoming increasingly popular for training neural networks (NNs) to solve PDEs and empirically outperform their first-order counterparts in both speed and accuracy, the convergence theory for training such models is essentially confined to first-order methods. In this paper, we close this gap and develop a convergence analysis for the regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton methods. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the training dynamics converge in probability, with explicit rates, to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a Newton neural tangent kernel operator associated with the PDE. Although the limiting kernel operator admits no spectral gap, we prove that, in the overparameterized limit, the PDE residual vanishes as training proceeds, and, under mild assumptions, the NN converges to the PDE solution. We further show that, provided a sufficiently small regularization parameter, the projection of the residual onto any fixed number of leading eigenfunctions decays exponentially fast, demonstrating that this hyperparameter acts as a spectral filter: it lifts the convergence rates of high-frequency components toward those of low-frequency ones, thereby mitigating the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. Mathematical challenges arise from the implicit parameter update involving a linear system whose dimension increases with the NN width and, for Newton's method, a potentially indefinite Hessian, as well as from the PDE operator entering the kernel.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Riedl, Justin Sirignano, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos

item.title: Square-root comparison, Turnpike, and exact semidefinite feasibility
item.description: arXiv:2611.34535v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given positive integers $a_i,K$, put $S=\sum_{i=1}^k\sqrt{a_i}$. We construct a realizable Turnpike instance in which the minimum spacing of distinct distances and the smallest nonzero addition residual are both at most $|S-K|$ when $S\ne K$. With approximation oracles, one three-distance realizability query decides $S\le K$. For unordered lists of radical sums with nonnegative rational coefficients, a polynomial-time substitution by integers preserves every normalized ruler. We give the classical reduction of square-root comparison to exact semidefinite feasibility in both threshold directions. The comparison enters through numerical separation and marked sorting; the integer recoding needs no such comparison for unordered reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: C. S. Elder

item.title: $\mu$MPC: Microsecond-Scale Nonlinear and World Model Control from Edge to GPU via Koopman-Linearized Precompilation
item.description: arXiv:2611.34597v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present $\mu$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $\mu$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $\mu$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23\mu$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $\mu$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.
item.dc:creator: Devesh Nath, Glen Chou

item.title: Boundary Observability for a Class of Degenerate Kolmogorov-Type Equations in a Cylindrical Domain
item.description: arXiv:2611.34679v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper investigates the boundary observability for a class of multi-dimensional degenerate Kolmogorov-type kinetic equations in a cylindrical domain $\Omega = \mathbb{T}_{x_1} \times (0,1)_{x_2}$. The model features a horizontal drift term $x_2^\gamma \partial_{x_1} \varphi$ coupled with a boundary-degenerate diffusion operator $\partial_{x_2}(x_2^\alpha \partial_{x_2} \varphi)$ acting solely on the velocity variable, where $\gamma = 1$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$. By leveraging the structural advantages of the cylindrical domain, we establish an analytical framework based on the method of separation of variables. Crucial Carleman estimates tailored to the degenerate dual operator are derived to capture the subtle dissipation effects under the influence of the transport term. Consequently, by virtue of a uniform a priori estimate, we establish the quantitative boundary observability inequality for the state function.
item.dc:creator: Dong-Hui Yang, Mengze Gu, Yuanzhi Zhou, Ghadir Shokor

item.title: From NP-Hardness to Exact Tractability Through Sample Abundance
item.description: arXiv:2611.34734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Additional observations can make exact optimization tractable without changing the objective or feasible set. We establish this phenomenon for noisy parity fitting, a worst-case NP-hard problem, with uniformly sampled rank-one sign tensor entries, independent fair factor signs and independent errors. For fixed interaction order $k\ge3$, $n$ signs per block, logarithmic mean degree and known channel biases, $O(n/(\log n)^{1/(k-2)})$ further readings of the same source suffice with high probability for exact optimization in $O(n\log^2 n)$ worst-case work. The leading coefficient is sharp for weak recovery by depth-$O(\log\log n)$ local estimators with independent reading marks. A common signed-field law determines the gain over the generating source, the number of tied optima and the dimension needed for later reweightings. The geometry of the remaining coordinates determines the sharp radius of local verification for high-scoring assignments with high probability.
item.dc:creator: Mojtaba Soltanalian

item.title: Time-optimal travel driven by two vector fields on a Riemannian manifold
item.description: arXiv:2611.34761v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study minimum-time travel on a Riemannian manifold $(M,h)$ for a kinematic model in which finitely many drift fields contribute additively to the velocity, after independent rescaling of their components parallel and orthogonal to a chosen unit direction $u$. The velocity is then $\mathcal Y_x(u)=(\eta(x)+h_x(\widehat Z_x,u))u+\widehat W_x$, $u\in UT_xM$, for two effective vector fields $\widehat Z$, $\widehat W$ and a self-propulsion speed $\eta\geq0$. Let $F$ be the gauge of the radial hull $\mathcal B_x=[0,1]\cdot\mathcal S_x$ of the velocity set $\mathcal S_x=\mathcal Y_x(UT_xM)$. Where $\eta>0$, we characterize when $F$ is a Finsler metric and give two-sided estimates and representation formulae for it; where $\eta=0$ and $\widehat Z\neq0$, we recover the Randers, Kropina and strong-wind regimes of Zermelo navigation. Examples include Matsumoto's slope metric, traction-modified slope models, and alternative models for wildfire propagation and microswimmer navigation. Since $F$ need not be a Finsler metric, we treat the minimum-time problem with tools from differential inclusions. For distinct endpoints, the inclusions defined by $\mathcal S_x$ and $\mathcal B_x$ give the same infimum travel time, and so does the convex hull of $\mathcal B_x$ under local controllability at the terminal point. When $F$ is finite, the infimum is attained if $(M,h)$ is complete, $\mathcal Y$ is bounded and each $\mathcal B_x$ is convex. When $F$ is a Finsler metric on $\{\eta>0\}$, the set $\{\eta=0\}$ cannot be reached from $\{\eta>0\}$ in finite time and, on $\{\eta>0\}$, the minimum time is the Finsler distance; if moreover $(M,h)$ is complete and $\eta$ is bounded, $F$ is forward and backward complete and the minimum time is attained by geodesics. We also compute the support Hamiltonian directly from the velocity law, for every $\eta\geq0$.
item.dc:creator: Erasmo Caponio, Dario Corona, Ebtsam H. Taha

item.title: Adaptive Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Singularly Perturbed Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.34866v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have emerged as a flexible and efficient approach for enforcing dynamic safety constraints. In this paper, we consider a class of uncertain nonlinear systems with singular perturbations and develop an adaptive CBF framework for such systems to enforce safety constraints on both the slow and fast subsystems in the overall singularly perturbed nonlinear system with uncertain parameters. We first develop a robustness property showing that if an adaptive controller for the slow subsystem satisfies the slow CBF condition with an appropriate safety margin, then for sufficiently small values of the singular perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$, the slow subsystem remains within an $O(\varepsilon)$-neighborhood of its safe set. We then consider the more general case of safety constraints on both the fast and slow subsystems and provide conditions under which joint slow-fast safety is achieved despite the parametric uncertainties. The reduced-order slow model and the slow and fast CBF conditions are evaluated using an online parameter estimate and the parameter mismatch between the estimated and true reduced-order models is addressed via a state-dependent robustness margin in the CBF inequalities. To illustrate the proposed framework, we present simulation studies for two systems with parametric uncertainties: a synthetic two-time-scale fourth-order example system and a unicycle with a fast turn-rate actuator and an obstacle avoidance safety constraint.
item.dc:creator: Prashanth Krishnamurthy, Farshad Khorrami

item.title: A note on mean field games of controls with state constraints: existence of mild solutions
item.description: arXiv:2109.11655v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show the existence of mild solutions for a first-order mean field game of controls under the state constraint that trajectories be confined in a closed and bounded set in euclidean space. This extends the results of Cannarsa and Capuani to the case of a mean field game of controls. Our controls are velocities and we find that the existence of an equilibrium is complicated by the requirement that they should have enough regularity. We solve this by imposing a small Lipschitz constant on the dependence of the Lagrangian on the joint measure of states and controls.
item.dc:creator: Jameson Graber, Sergio Mayorga

item.title: Neur2BiLO: Neural Bilevel Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2402.02552v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bilevel optimization deals with nested problems in which a leader takes the first decision to minimize their objective function while accounting for a follower's best-response reaction. Constrained bilevel problems with integer variables are particularly notorious for their hardness. While exact solvers have been proposed for mixed-integer linear bilevel optimization, they tend to scale poorly with problem size and are hard to generalize to the non-linear case. On the other hand, problem-specific algorithms (exact and heuristic) are limited in scope. Under a data-driven setting in which similar instances of a bilevel problem are solved routinely, our proposed framework, Neur2BiLO, embeds a neural network approximation of the leader's or follower's value function, trained via supervised regression, into an easy-to-solve mixed-integer program. Neur2BiLO serves as a heuristic that produces high-quality solutions extremely fast for four applications with linear and non-linear objectives and pure and mixed-integer variables.
item.dc:creator: Justin Dumouchelle, Esther Julien, Jannis Kurtz, Elias B. Khalil

item.title: Stability Regularized Cross-Validation
item.description: arXiv:2505.06927v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study hyperparameter selection via cross-validation, motivated by settings in which the selected $k$-fold cross-validation error underestimates the selected model's test error. We propose a nested $k$-fold cross-validation scheme that minimizes a weighted sum of the standard cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, with the stability weight selected by an outer cross-validation loop. We derive a generalization bound that controls test error using the cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, together with correction terms common to every candidate. In a stylized ridge regression setting, we then show that whether the stability weight improves expected test-set performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, with the greatest improvement when the signal-to-noise ratio is small. On $13$ real-world regression datasets, the procedure reduces the average out-of-sample MSE relative to $k$-fold cross-validation by $5.6\%$ for sparse regression and by $6.8\%$ for CART. A side benefit of an outer cross-validation loop is that the selected error estimates are better calibrated than those from ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation: the error estimate moves from 12.3\% below the selected test-set MSE to 5.8\% above it for sparse regression and from 10.3\% below to 0.2\% above it for CART.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Cory-Wright, Andr\'es G\'omez

item.title: Mirror descent for constrained stochastic control problems
item.description: arXiv:2506.02564v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mirror descent is a well established tool for solving convex optimization problems with convex constraints. This article introduces continuous-time mirror descent dynamics for approximating optimal Markov controls for stochastic control problems with the action space being bounded and convex. We show that if the Hamiltonian is uniformly convex in its action variable then mirror descent converges linearly while if it is uniformly strongly convex relative to an appropriate Bregman divergence, then the mirror flow converges exponentially. The two fundamental difficulties that must be overcome to prove such results are: first, the inherent lack of convexity of the map from Markov controls to the corresponding value function. Second, maintaining sufficient regularity of the value function and the Markov controls along the mirror descent updates. The first issue is handled using the performance difference lemma, while the second using careful Sobolev space estimates for the solutions of the associated linear PDEs. Finally, we complement the theoretical analysis with numerical experiments. We provide a model-based algorithm which uses finite difference discretization and discrete mirror descent updates. Empirical results confirm the theoretically predicted convergence rates. We also provide a model-free algorithm which uses martingale differences to learn the advantage rate function and applies this in the mirror descent updates of the policy.
item.dc:creator: Deven Sethi, David \v{S}i\v{s}ka

item.title: Sensitivity to Information Channel and Model Perturbations in Partially Observable Stochastic Control
item.description: arXiv:2508.10658v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Studying the stability of partially observed Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with respect to perturbations in the transition and observation kernels is a significant problem. While asymptotic robustness/stability results, as approximate transition kernels and/or measurement kernels converge to the true ones, have been previously reported, explicit bounds on value differences and mismatch costs have been limited in scope for POMDPs. The main technical contribution of this paper is a collection of explicit and uniform bounds on the distance between the filter kernels (that is, the kernels of the belief-MDP reduction) of two POMDPs, in the bounded-Lipschitz and Wasserstein metrics, in terms of the total variation and Wasserstein distances between their transition and measurement kernels; we also establish the sharpness of these bounds, demonstrate through counterexamples that the metrics employed cannot be weakened, and present verifiable conditions, stated directly in terms of the defining system functions, under which they apply. Building on these kernel proximity bounds, we show that control policies optimized for approximate models yield explicit performance guarantees when applied to the true model, under both discounted and average cost criteria. Two settings are treated separately: policy transfer, where the controller knows the true model and only the policy is designed for the approximate one, and model misspecification, where the controller also computes its beliefs with the approximate model. As a particular application, we consider the case where the state space and the measurement spaces are quantized to obtain finite models, and we obtain explicit error bounds which decay to zero as the approximations get finer. This provides explicit performance guarantees for model reduction in POMDPs.
item.dc:creator: Yunus Emre Demirci, Ali Devran Kara, Serdar Y\"uksel

item.title: Zeroth-order Algorithms for Distributed Online Optimization against Byzantine Edge Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2511.05104v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Byzantine attacks pose a fundamental challenge to distributed optimization, especially when they occur on communication edges, where truthful and corrupted messages coexist and attacked links are difficult to identify. While most existing studies focus on time-invariant objectives, many practical systems operate in dynamic environments and require distributed online optimization under such attacks. A central question is whether sublinear dynamic regret, a benchmark performance in online optimization, can still be achieved under Byzantine edge attacks. This paper answers this question affirmatively. We directly study distributed online optimization with time-varying directed networks, where the identities of adversarial edges are unknown to the agents and may change over time, and only zeroth-order feedback is available. Two resilient algorithms are proposed based on randomized and deterministic zeroth-order schemes. The former is more query-efficient and requires weaker smoothness conditions, while the latter provides deterministic guarantees and better performance in simulations. Both algorithms achieve consensus and, under suitable minimizer-path variation and algorithmic parameter conditions, achieve sublinear dynamic regret with respect to the original unweighted sum of local losses, without imposing stochastic assumptions for losses. Numerical results validate the theoretical findings. Overall, the results show that reliable distributed online optimization remains possible even under complex Byzantine edge attacks and limited feedback.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Liu, Yujie Tang, Wenjun Mei

item.title: A Solution Concept for Convex Vector Optimization Problems based on a User-defined Region of Interest
item.description: arXiv:2603.26305v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work addresses arbitrary convex vector optimization problems, which constitute a general framework for multi-criteria decision-making in diverse real-world applications. Due to their complexity, such problems are typically tackled using polyhedral approximation. Existing solution concepts rely on additional assumptions, such as boundedness, polyhedrality of the ordering cone, or existence of interior points in the ordering cone, and typically focus on absolute error measures. We introduce a solution concept based on the homogenization of the upper image that employs relative error measures and avoids additional structural assumptions. Although minimality is not explicitly required, a form of approximate weak minimality is implicitly ensured under attainability. The concept is straightforward, requiring only a single precision parameter and, owing to relative errors, remains robust under scaling of the target functions. Homogenization also eliminates the need for the binary distinction between points far from the origin and directions which can lead to numerical difficulties. Furthermore, in practice decision-makers often identify a region where preferred solutions are expected. Our concept supports both a global overview of the upper image and a refined local perspective within such a user-defined region of interest (RoI). We present a decision-making procedure enabling iterative refinement of this region and the associated preferences.
item.dc:creator: Daniel D\"orfler, Rebecca K\"ohler, Andreas L\"ohne

item.title: Optimal control of symmetry-breaking dynamics near criticality
item.description: arXiv:2607.16188v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of optimal control for dynamical systems near a pitchfork bifurcation, motivated by the role of external cues in guiding symmetry-breaking transitions in cell-fate selection and other natural processes. Using an asymptotic expansion of the optimality conditions obtained from the Pontryagin maximum principle, the leading-order optimal control law for a general n-dimensional system is examined across three dynamical regimes distinguished by scaling of control strength with respect to the distance from criticality. While in the strong control limit the results reduce to known approximations from linear-quadratic control, we derive generalized amplitude equations for the co-evolution of state and costate variables describing the optimized trajectory in the weak and intermediate control regimes. These control normal forms are validated against numerical solutions of the full optimal control problem for a canonical model of a bistable biochemical switch. The bifurcation structure of the optimal control problem is analyzed in the weak control regime. Finally, we demonstrate the construction of asymptotic solutions in the long time limit in this regime using boundary-layer methods.
item.dc:creator: Pearson W. Miller

item.title: Reflected Schr\"odinger Bridge Problem over Noncharacteristic Sub-Riemannian Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2607.17904v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We formulate and solve the reflected sub-Riemannian Schr\"odinger problem: minimum-energy transport of probability distributions for underactuated dynamics with degenerate diffusion on a bounded domain. Since Euclidean normal reflection is generally incompatible with the horizontal subbundle, we construct an intrinsic reflection field from the geometry of the diffusion; it is well-defined when the boundary is non-characteristic, structurally delimiting the theory. Under appropriate assumptions, we establish the existence of a smooth, positive transition density for the reference law, and the optimal control is characterized by a mild Schr\"odinger system with asymmetric boundary conditions, determined by the reflection field, Popp measure, sub-Riemannian fields and It\^o drift. This characterization yields a PDE-based Sinkhorn iteration that enforces these conditions directly, without evaluating the unavailable transition kernel.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Owusu Adu

item.title: Global Exponential and Inverse Optimal Stabilization of a 3D Nonholonomic Vehicle in Spherical Coordinates
item.description: arXiv:2609.24192v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For the 3D nonholonomic vehicle actuated in surge velocity, pitch rate, and yaw rate, we construct continuous time-invariant feedback laws that stabilize both the roll-free and roll-augmented kinematic models to a target position and orientation in spherical coordinates. The design uses a spherical coordinate transformation with a singular set of codimension two and measure zero. We first present a backstepping design that yields explicit unidirectional, cusp-free feedback laws and strict barrier control Lyapunov functions (CLFs). These establish global exponential stability in spherical coordinates with user-assigned decay rates, while ensuring bounded Cartesian trajectories and exponential convergence to the target, consistent with Brockett's obstruction. The barrier terms guarantee avoidance of the coordinate singularities away from the target. The strict CLFs are then used to develop families of asymptotically stabilizing inverse optimal feedback laws for both systems that minimize a meaningful infinite-horizon cost. These laws inherit infinite gain margins from driftlessness, respect user-defined input bounds through Legendre-Fenchel transformations, and are implementable with either bidirectional or unidirectional surge actuation. Two penalty choices are illustrated: a quadratic input penalty whose associated state running cost approaches a prescribed quadratic form, and an input-constraining penalty that enforces user-defined bounds. This paper lays the foundation for constructive stabilization of the 3D nonholonomic vehicle.
item.dc:creator: Kwang Hak Kim, Velimir Todorovski, Mamadou Diagne, Miroslav Krstic

item.title: Closing the Accuracy Gap in Stochastic First-Order Bilevel Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.03633v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the stochastic first-order complexity of smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel optimization with fresh, conditionally unbiased gradient samples of bounded variance. We assume globally $L$-Lipschitz gradients, bounded $f_y$, $\mu$-strong convexity of the lower objective, and $\rho$-Lipschitz lower Hessian blocks. Let $\kappa=L/\mu$, $\vartheta=\rho/\mu$, and $\chi=1+\vartheta$. For $\kappa\ge2$, $1\le\vartheta\le\kappa^2$, every initial-gap budget $\Delta>0$, and $0<\epsilon\le c\min\{L,\sqrt{L\Delta}\}$, we establish $\mathsf{T}_{\mathrm{SFO}}(\epsilon)=\widetilde{\Theta}(L\chi\kappa^{5/2}\Delta\epsilon^{-2}+L\kappa^4\sigma_f^2\Delta\epsilon^{-4}+L^3\vartheta^2\chi\kappa^8\sigma_g^2\Delta\epsilon^{-6})$, where $\sigma_f^2$ and $\sigma_g^2$ are the upper- and lower-level variance budgets. The comparison assumes a finite lower-initialization certificate, holds uniformly over both nonnegative noise budgets, and uses an accuracy constant $c$ independent of conditioning. Three lower-bound families capture the deterministic, upper-noise, and lower-noise contributions. The bounds cover arbitrary randomized adaptive queries and terminal outputs under worst-case expected costs, even for conservative sample gradients. The upper bound combines accelerated frozen-linear-tilt solves with displacement-based reuse of the full upper gradient. An independently chosen base-chain length yields the uniform accuracy range, while a projection and homotopy argument separates undisclosed coordinates from a newly disclosed source, allowing $\vartheta/\kappa$ to grow without bound. The bounds match polynomial orders and noise transitions; exact logarithmic exponents and coarser accuracies remain open.
item.dc:creator: Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Yanyi Li, Chunyuan Zheng, Cong Fang, Haoxuan Li, Zhouchen Lin

item.title: Douglas--Rachford Algorithm with Relaxed Resolvents
item.description: arXiv:2611.21377v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper we study the convergence of a generalization of the Douglas--Rachford algorithm for finding a zero of the sum of two maximally monotone operators, where reflected resolvents are extended to relaxed resolvents. This extension allows for different step sizes in the resolvents under cocoercivity. We show that the resulting method converges weakly when its parameters lie in a range determined by the cocoercivity constants, which reduces to the classical algorithm when these constants vanish. Our main results concern the cocoercive case when one of the operators is in addition strongly monotone, in which the composition is a strict contraction. For both monotone inclusions and convex minimization, we compute the contraction factor and its optimal parameters in closed form, and show that the resulting rates are tight. Whenever the second operator is cocoercive, the optimal rates are strictly smaller than the corresponding rates of forward-backward splitting and of the classical Peaceman--Rachford and Douglas--Rachford algorithms and, in convex minimization, than those of FISTA. All theoretical rates are corroborated by the numerical worst cases obtained via performance estimation.
item.dc:creator: Luis Brice\~no-Arias, Fernando Rold\'an, Adrien Taylor

item.title: A note on approximate projection onto the semidefinite complementarity set
item.description: arXiv:2611.29199v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The proximal slack update in an augmented Lagrangian method for semidefinite complementarity constraints requires a joint matrix projection. Given real symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$, we seek the nearest pair $(X,Z)$ with $X$ positive semidefinite, $Z$ negative semidefinite, and $XZ=0$. Hou, Peng and Ding obtain a squared-loss factor of $2$ by fitting the pair in an eigenbasis of $A+B$. To improve this bound, we replace the orthogonal projector onto the subspace allowed for $X$ by a symmetric matrix $T$ with eigenvalues in $[0,1]$. From an optimal solution of the resulting semidefinite program, we form candidate subspaces by starting at the zero subspace and adding the eigenspaces of $T$ in decreasing order of eigenvalue. For each candidate, we compress $A$ to that subspace and $B$ to its orthogonal complement. We keep the positive eigenvalues of the first compression and the negative eigenvalues of the second. The best pair has squared loss at most $1.189$ times the minimum for arbitrary inputs and at most $1.15487$ times the minimum when $A$ is positive semidefinite and $B$ is negative semidefinite. For arbitrary inputs the factor improves to $1.18$ if $T$ has at most two distinct eigenvalues in $(0,1)$. The threshold-rounding proofs average over a uniform spectral threshold and use computer-assisted bounds for the resulting scalar inequalities.
item.dc:creator: Chao Ding

item.title: Iterated harmonic envelopes for multidimensional optimal stopping
item.description: arXiv:2505.09725v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motivated by the contrast between the classical least-concave-majorant representation of Dynkin and Yushkevich in one dimension and the substantially more complicated potential-theoretic structure of optimal stopping in higher dimensions, we identify a fundamental barrier: a localisation obstruction caused by the geometry of Brownian paths in dimensions $d\ge2$. We overcome it with an iterative construction based on harmonic-function envelopes, each an infimum of harmonic replacements on subdomains of the current non-contact set, with the previous envelope as boundary data. From a continuous gain function $g$, this produces a decreasing sequence of upper bounds $w_n$ converging uniformly to the value function $V$ of optimal stopping. The process may be Brownian motion or, more generally, any diffusion with a short list of properties, including polarity of points. For Brownian motion, every iterate inherits the modulus of continuity of the data. Exponential discounting may be included, and the state space may be a bounded regular domain with absorption at the boundary, or the whole space under a condition at infinity. Equivalently, the iterates converge to the solution of the associated obstacle problem. At each iteration an explicit stopping rule gives a lower bound for $V$. Both bounds are computed from the construction alone, without knowledge of $V$, and their gap falls below any given threshold after finitely many iterations. The first exit time from the limit non-contact set is optimal.
item.dc:creator: John Moriarty

item.title: Derivative Estimation from Coarse, Irregular, Noisy Samples: An MLE-Spline Approach
item.description: arXiv:2507.22176v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We address numerical differentiation under coarse, non-uniform sampling and Gaussian noise. A maximum-likelihood estimator with $L_2$-norm constraint on a higher-order derivative is obtained, yielding spline-based solution.
